Let's verify: Suppose a triangle with angles (A, B, C). Cut from the A-vertex to a point P on the opposite side (BC). The cut splits angle A into x and A−x. The two resulting triangles: one contains vertex B, the other vertex C. The triangle containing B has angles: at A: x (or A−x), at B: B, at the new vertex P: 180 − B − x. Hmm, wait. Let me think.

Triangle ABC with angles A at vertex A, B at vertex B, C at vertex C. Cut from A to point P on side BC. The two triangles are ABP and APC. Triangle ABP: angles at A is x (angle BAP), at B is B, at P is 180 − x − B. Triangle APC: angles at A is A−x, at C is C, at P is 180 − (A−x) − C. Note that the angles at P in the two triangles sum to 180 (since AP is a straight line through P on BC... wait, actually P is on BC, so the angles at P are ∠APB and ∠APC, which sum to 180). Indeed 180 − x − B + 180 − (A−x) − C = 360 − (A+B+C) = 360 − 180 = 180. Good.

So triangle ABP has angles (x, B, 180 − x − B) and triangle APC has (A−x, C, 180 − (A−x) − C) = (A−x, C, B + x). Hmm: 180 − (A−x) − C = 180 − A + x − C = (B) + x since A + B + C = 180 → 180 − A − C = B. So the P-angle in triangle APC is B + x. And the P angle in ABP is 180 − x − B = A + C − x.

So the two triples: (x, B, A + C − x) and (A − x, C, B + x). This matches the write-up: "(B, x, A+C−x) and (C, A−x, B+x)". Yes, that's correct as a reformulation. But it's just a reformulation, no result.
